---
title: Calder Valley Regional Library System, circulation and facilities study, fiscal 2026
type: source
---

## Scope

The board of the Calder Valley Regional Library System commissioned this study in
September 2025 and received it in July 2026. CVRL serves 11 towns and a service population
of 214,000 people from 14 branches, a technical services center, and a delivery van route
that connects them. The study covers fiscal 2019 through fiscal 2026 and was asked to
answer one question: which branches, if any, should close, and what would close with them.

The 14 branches are Ardmore Hollow, Bell Quarry, Cass Field, Dunmoor, Ferris Bend, Gullick,
Harrow Mill, Innis Park, Jarvey Street, Kestrel Landing, Lyle Crossing, Munce Road,
Norbeck, and Petrel Street. A fifteenth branch, Eastlin, closed in 2022 and is treated in
this study as a precedent rather than as part of the current system.

The study was prepared by Pell Lundgren Associates. Aurelio Pinter led the work and signed
the recommendations. Renata Okonjo, the system director, supplied the circulation and
staffing data. Marisol Deeb chairs the board and set the terms of the engagement, including
the instruction that the study consider at least one alternative to closure for every
closure it proposes.

## Method

Circulation figures come from the system's catalog and are counted as items checked out,
with a renewal counted as a checkout, which is the convention CVRL has used since 2014.
Door counts come from infrared counters at each entrance and are halved to correct for
double counting, a correction the study notes is standard and imprecise. Program
attendance is counted by hand by the staff member running the program.

Cost per branch is the sum of branch staff salaries and benefits, utilities, maintenance,
and a share of system overhead allocated by square footage. The study flags this
allocation as the number most open to argument, because overhead allocated to a closed
branch does not disappear when the branch does.

Patron survey data comes from an intercept survey conducted in October 2025 at all 14
branches. The survey reached 1,200 patrons. It was administered in person on weekdays and
Saturdays, and the study states plainly that a weekday intercept survey undercounts people
who cannot visit on a weekday.

## Circulation, fiscal 2019 through fiscal 2026

Total circulation across the system was 1,400,000 items in fiscal 2019 and 1,120,000 items
in fiscal 2026, a decline of 20 percent over seven years. The headline number hides a
split. Physical circulation, meaning books, media, and everything else that moves on the
delivery van, fell 31 percent over the same stretch. Digital circulation, meaning ebooks
and downloadable audio, rose 84 percent.

Digital was 14 percent of total circulation in fiscal 2019 and 38 percent in fiscal 2026.
The study projects, without much confidence, that digital passes half of total circulation
somewhere between fiscal 2029 and fiscal 2032, and notes that digital circulation costs
the system more per item than physical circulation does, because the licenses expire and
the copies have to be bought again.

Active cardholders, defined as a card used at least once in the preceding year, numbered
96,000 in fiscal 2026. The system issued 31,000 new cards that year, the highest new card
count in the study period, which sits awkwardly beside the circulation decline. Pinter
offers no explanation for the two figures moving in opposite directions and recommends
that the system look into it.

The system filled 78,000 holds in fiscal 2026. Of those, 26 percent moved an item from one
branch to another on the delivery van. The study treats that 26 percent as evidence the
branches operate as one collection rather than as 14 collections, and as an argument that
closing a branch does not remove its users' access to the items that branch held.

## Visits and programs

Door counts fell further than circulation. The system counted 986,000 visits in fiscal 2019
and 640,000 in fiscal 2026, a decline of 35 percent. The steepest single year was fiscal
2021. Visits recovered after that but have not returned to the fiscal 2019 level at any
branch except Norbeck and Kestrel Landing.

Programs run against the trend. CVRL ran 2,400 programs in fiscal 2026 with 61,000 people
attending. Program attendance is up 19 percent since fiscal 2022. Storytime and homework
help account for most of the attendance. The study observes that program attendance is the
only public-facing measure rising across the system, and that the measure the board has
historically reported to the towns is circulation.

## The four branches under review

The study applies a screen: a branch enters the closure review if its circulation is under
15,000 items a year, or its cost per circulated item is more than double the system
average, or its building carries deferred maintenance worth more than a quarter of its
assessed value. Four branches met at least one of those conditions. The system average
cost per circulated item in fiscal 2026 was 16 dollars.

### Gullick

Gullick is the smallest branch in the system. The building went up in 1931 as a grange
hall and was given to the town in 1968. It holds 2,200 square feet. The branch is open 18
hours a week across three days, staffed by one full-time librarian and two part-time
assistants, and circulated 9,400 items in fiscal 2026.

Gullick costs 570,000 dollars a year to operate, which works out to 61 dollars per
circulated item, close to four times the system average. The building carries 1,300,000
dollars of deferred maintenance, most of it a roof replacement and a boiler that the
facilities report describes as past the end of its service life and running.

Tomas Vry manages the branch. His written response to the draft study makes two points.
The first is that Gullick's 18 hours are the fewest in the system and that circulation per
open hour at Gullick is higher than at Munce Road, which is open 32 hours. The second is
that the 1,300,000 dollar maintenance figure assumes the building is kept as a library, and
that the town has asked twice about taking the building back.

### Dunmoor

Dunmoor circulated 12,000 items in fiscal 2026 at a cost of 380,000 dollars, or 32 dollars
per item, twice the system average. The branch is open 24 hours a week. The building is
sound and was renovated in 2015, which is why it fails the circulation screen and passes
the facilities screen.

The case against closing Dunmoor is distance. The nearest other branch is Harrow Mill, 14
miles away by road. The bus route between them runs four times a day and takes 52 minutes.
The study states that 41 percent of Dunmoor's surveyed users arrived on foot or by bus and
that the system has no measure of how many of them would reach Harrow Mill.

### Bell Quarry

Bell Quarry entered the review on cost per item and is the study's clearest argument
against the screen it used. The branch circulated 41,000 items in fiscal 2026, which is
respectable, but it is open 46 hours a week and carries the second highest staffing cost in
the system, so its cost per circulated item is 29 dollars.

Bell Quarry also ran the largest program calendar in the system, with 11,000 people
attending programs there in fiscal 2026, 18 percent of the system total. Counting only
circulation, Bell Quarry looks expensive. Counting programs, it is the busiest building
CVRL operates. Pinter recommends removing Bell Quarry from the closure list and revising
the screen so that a branch's program attendance counts in the denominator.

### Norbeck

Norbeck circulated 13,000 items in fiscal 2026 at 27 dollars per item. The building is
leased, and the lease runs to 2031 with no early termination, so closing the branch saves
the staffing cost and none of the occupancy cost. That alone takes Norbeck off the list on
arithmetic.

The survey adds a second reason. Among Norbeck's surveyed users, 73 percent reported no
home broadband, the highest share at any branch, and 58 percent of Norbeck visits in the
survey week were for the public computers rather than for materials. Norbeck is one of two
branches where visits have returned to the fiscal 2019 level.

## The Eastlin precedent

Eastlin closed in June 2022 after a board vote of 7 to 4. It had 1,600 active cardholders
at the time and circulated 16,000 items in its final full year. The closure was projected
to save 310,000 dollars a year, and the study confirms that the system's costs fell by
roughly that amount.

What happened to Eastlin's users is the part the study treats as the finding. CVRL tracked
the 1,600 cards for the year following the closure. Circulation by those cardholders fell
44 percent. Only 29 percent of them registered at another branch. The rest either stopped
using the system or used it only through the digital catalog, and the study cannot separate
those two groups with the data it has.

Pinter writes that the Eastlin result is the single most important number in the study and
the one the board has never been shown. The projected savings were real. The projection
assumed that displaced users would turn up somewhere else in the system, and most of them
did not. The study frames this as a cost moved off the ledger rather than removed, because
a lost cardholder still lives in a town that pays the levy.

## Savings if Gullick and Dunmoor close

Pinter's closure recommendation is limited to Gullick and Dunmoor. Their combined operating
cost is 950,000 dollars a year. The study estimates that 640,000 dollars of that is
genuinely avoidable, with the remainder being collections, cataloging, and system overhead
that continues whether the branches are open or not.

Of the 640,000 dollars, 47 percent is staff cost, and the study assumes those staff are
reassigned to fill vacancies elsewhere rather than laid off, which is the board's stated
practice. On that assumption the net annual saving is 340,000 dollars against an operating
budget of 18,000,000 dollars. The study states the ratio plainly: the closures save under
two percent of the budget.

One-time costs cut into that further. Moving and absorbing the two collections is estimated
at 120,000 dollars, and the Gullick building, if the town does not take it back, carries
mothballing costs the study does not estimate.

## The facilities backlog

The system carries 24,000,000 dollars of deferred maintenance across its 14 buildings. Six
buildings account for 78 percent of it. Gullick is one of the six. Closing Gullick removes
1,300,000 dollars from the backlog, or 5 percent of it, and the study is careful to say
that removing a number from a backlog is not the same as funding the rest of it.

The facilities report underlying this section was completed in March 2026 and rates each
building on four systems: roof, envelope, mechanical, and electrical. Three buildings rate
poor on two or more systems. The study recommends a capital plan before any closure
decision, on the grounds that a board choosing between branches without knowing what the
remaining buildings need is choosing with half the information.

## Staffing

CVRL employed 214 people in fiscal 2019 and employs 187 now, a loss of 27 FTE positions.
The vacancy rate stood at 12 percent in June 2026, and the system paid for 18,000 hours of
substitute coverage in fiscal 2026 to keep advertised hours. The study notes that the
substitute hours are what makes the vacancy rate survivable and that they cost more per
hour than the positions they cover.

Okonjo's staffing memo, included as an appendix, argues that the system is already
operating two branches below its stated staffing standard and that a closure decision made
now would be read by staff as ratifying the vacancies. Pinter does not respond to this
point in the recommendations.

## Collections and spending

The collections budget was 1,900,000 dollars in fiscal 2019 and 1,480,000 dollars in
fiscal 2026, a decline of 22 percent. New physical items added to the collection fell from
38,000 a year to 21,000 a year over the same period, a drop of 45 percent, which is
steeper than the budget decline because per-item prices rose.

Digital licensing took 520,000 dollars in fiscal 2026, or 35 percent of the collections
budget, up from 11 percent in fiscal 2019. A typical ebook license costs the system 55
dollars and expires after 24 checkouts or two years, whichever comes first. The study
points out that a physical copy bought in fiscal 2019 is still on a shelf and a digital
copy bought in fiscal 2019 is gone, and that the circulation figures treat the two as the
same event.

Pinter flags one consequence for the closure question. A branch's circulation depends on
what the system bought, and the system bought 45 percent fewer new physical items than it
did seven years ago. A small branch with a thin new-materials shelf will show a
circulation decline that looks like a demand problem and is at least partly a purchasing
decision made at the system level.

## The delivery van and the shared collection

The delivery van runs five days a week and covers 190 miles a day, reaching every branch
once each weekday. It costs 210,000 dollars a year to operate. It carried the 78,000 holds
counted earlier, and the median hold at CVRL fills in 11 days.

The study uses the van to argue both sides. If the collection is genuinely shared, then a
Gullick patron losing a branch does not lose access to the items, only to the building.
That argument holds only if the patron reaches another building, and the Eastlin tracking
says most of them did not. The study calls the van a partial answer to the access question
and an incomplete one.

Vry's response notes a third point about the van: closing two branches removes two stops
from the route, which the study counts as no saving at all, since the van runs whether it
stops at 12 buildings or 14.

## Peer comparison

Pell Lundgren compared CVRL against three regional systems of similar size in neighboring
counties. Their total circulation declines over the same seven years were 17 percent, 23
percent, and 29 percent. CVRL's 20 percent sits inside that band and below the midpoint of
it.

Two of the three peer systems closed a branch during the period. One of the two reported
tracking its displaced cardholders and found a 38 percent drop in their circulation, close
to the 44 percent CVRL measured after Eastlin. The study treats the agreement between two
independent measurements as the strongest evidence in the document, while noting that two
observations are not a trend.

The peer comparison does not settle the closure question. What it settles, the study
argues, is whether CVRL's decline is a local failure of management. It is not: the system
is losing circulation at about the rate its neighbors are, with a smaller collections
budget than two of the three.

## Public comment

The board held 11 hearings between February and May 2026. The record counts 340 speakers.
Coded by position, 62 percent opposed any closure, 21 percent supported closing specific
branches, and the remainder took no position or spoke to an unrelated matter.

Hattie Bream of Norbeck spoke at four hearings and is quoted in the study: the question is
not whether the numbers are right, it is which numbers the board agreed to count. The study
includes the line without comment.

Attendance at the hearings was itself uneven. Three of the 11 hearings drew fewer than ten
speakers, and all three were held in towns with no branch under review.

## Alternatives

The study costs three alternatives to closure, as the engagement required.

Reducing open hours by four a week at all 14 branches saves 410,000 dollars a year, more
than the closures net, and the study calls this the option the board will like least
because it makes every town slightly worse off instead of two towns much worse off.

A bookmobile serving Gullick, Dunmoor, and four other low-circulation areas costs 280,000
dollars a year to run, including the vehicle amortized over 12 years. The study cannot say
what it would circulate, because CVRL has never run one.

Merging technical services with the neighboring system saves 190,000 dollars a year and
takes about 18 months to implement. The study rates this the lowest risk of the three and
notes that it has been proposed twice before and not acted on.

## What the study does not answer

Three questions are named as out of scope or unanswerable with current data.

The study cannot say what circulation the system would have had without the branch
closures and hour reductions already made since fiscal 2019, because there is no
counterfactual and no comparable system to benchmark against.

It cannot say whether the 31 percent decline in physical circulation is a change in demand
or a change in supply. The collections budget fell 22 percent over the same period, and
the study observes that a system buying fewer copies will circulate fewer items, and that
the two effects cannot be separated in the data CVRL keeps.

It does not evaluate the towns' levy formula, which is the mechanism that would actually
determine whether a closure returns money to the town it closes in. Deeb ruled that
question out of scope at the start of the engagement. Pinter notes the exclusion in the
recommendations and states that it is the question every speaker at the hearings was
actually asking.
